title: Lesion Localization II: Cord, Roots & Nerves
summary: Localizing below the brain: spinal cord, roots, plexus, nerve, junction and muscle.

lessons.title: Myelopathy Patterns

levels.kid:
Your spinal cord is like a thick cable running down the middle of your back, safe inside the bones of your spine. It carries messages between your brain and your body.

If the cable gets squeezed or hurt at one spot, everything below that spot can have trouble. The legs might get weak or stiff, feeling might fade below a line on the belly, and the bladder might not work right.

Doctors look for that line where feeling changes. It tells them how high up the problem is, like finding which floor of a building has a broken elevator.
levels.hs:
**Myelopathy** means a problem in the spinal cord itself. It causes a mix of signs:
- **Upper motor neuron signs below the level**: weakness, stiffness (spasticity), brisk reflexes and Babinski signs.
- **A sensory level**: a line on the body below which sensation is reduced. Key landmarks: nipple line about T4, umbilicus about T10, groin about L1.
- **Bladder and bowel problems**: urgency, retention or incontinence.
- Sometimes **lower motor neuron signs at the level** of the lesion, because the cord's own motor neurons there are damaged.

Common causes:
- **Compression**: degenerative cervical spine disease (the most common cause in older adults), disc herniation, tumors (often metastases), abscess, or trauma.
- **Inflammation**: transverse myelitis, multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica.
- **Vascular**: spinal cord infarction (sudden), or a dural arteriovenous fistula (slowly worsening).
- **Metabolic**: vitamin B12 or copper deficiency affects the back (dorsal) columns and side tracts.

Partial cord syndromes have special patterns. In **Brown-Séquard syndrome** (half of the cord), the same side loses strength and vibration sense, while the opposite side loses pain and temperature.

Acute cord compression is a **neurosurgical emergency**: the sooner the pressure is relieved, the better the chance of recovery.
levels.college:
**Myelopathy recognition**: bilateral UMN signs below a level, a sensory level, sphincter dysfunction, and absence of cranial nerve or cortical signs. In cervical lesions, arms can show LMN signs at the lesion level (segmental) with UMN signs below.

**Cord syndromes**
- **Complete transection**: loss of all motor and sensory function below the level, with autonomic dysfunction.
- **Brown-Séquard (hemicord)**: ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration/proprioception; contralateral pain/temperature loss starting one to two segments below.
- **Central cord**: arms weaker than legs, variable sensory loss; classically after hyperextension injury in a stenotic cervical spine. A syrinx causes suspended dissociated loss (cape distribution) and segmental hand wasting.
- **Anterior cord** (anterior spinal artery infarct): paralysis and pain/temperature loss below the level with preserved vibration and proprioception (dorsal columns supplied by posterior spinal arteries).
- **Posterior cord**: loss of vibration and proprioception with sensory ataxia; B12, copper deficiency, tabes dorsalis.
- **Conus medullaris** (around L1): early sphincter dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, mixed UMN/LMN signs, often symmetric.
- **Cauda equina** (roots below L1–L2): asymmetric LMN leg weakness, radicular pain, areflexia, saddle anesthesia, retention.

**Time course and causes**: hyperacute (infarction, hemorrhage, trauma); acute/subacute over hours to days (transverse myelitis, epidural abscess, metastatic compression); chronic (spondylotic myelopathy, tumors, hereditary spastic paraplegia, dural AV fistula with stepwise worsening on exertion).

**Workup**: urgent MRI of the relevant spine with contrast, guided by the level; if the level is unclear, image the whole spine. Then CSF (inflammation), aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies, B12 and copper, and infection screening as indicated.
levels.phd:
Spinal cord syndromes reflect the cord's internal topography and its vascular supply, which together explain why particular patterns cluster with particular causes.

**Vascular anatomy.** A single anterior spinal artery supplies roughly the anterior two-thirds of the cord, reinforced by segmental radiculomedullary arteries; the largest, the artery of Adamkiewicz, usually enters on the left between T9 and T12. The upper thoracic cord has relatively sparse collateral supply, a vulnerable territory during hypotension or aortic surgery. Paired posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns, explaining dorsal column sparing in anterior cord infarction.

**Compressive myelopathy pathophysiology.** Degenerative cervical myelopathy combines static narrowing (disc-osteophyte complexes, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament) and dynamic injury during flexion-extension. Chronic compression produces ischemia, demyelination, apoptosis of oligodendrocytes, and endothelial disruption of the blood-spinal cord barrier. T2 hyperintensity on MRI reflects edema or gliosis, and T1 hypointensity suggests irreversible damage with worse prognosis.

**Inflammatory myelopathies.** Lesion length discriminates: multiple sclerosis typically causes short, peripherally located lesions spanning fewer than two vertebral segments, while neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin-4 IgG, an astrocytopathy) causes longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis over three or more segments, often central. MOG antibody disease frequently involves the conus and gray matter (the "H sign").

**Dural arteriovenous fistula.** Arterial blood shunts into the venous plexus, raising venous pressure and causing congestive myelopathy (Foix-Alajouanine syndrome in its advanced form). It often affects older men, worsens with exercise or posture changes, and is treatable by endovascular or surgical disconnection, making it an important can't-miss diagnosis.

**Spinal shock and recovery.** Acute transection yields areflexia that resolves over days to weeks as spinal circuits reorganize; persistent bulbocavernosus reflex return is classically used to mark the end of spinal shock. Plasticity research targets axonal regeneration barriers (Nogo, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) and epidural stimulation, which has restored some voluntary movement in experimental settings.
levels.expert:
Myelopathy is one of the commonest reasons a neurosurgeon is called urgently, and the clinical exam decides how fast the scanner and the operating room must move.

**What to do in the first hour**
- Confirm the pattern: bilateral leg UMN signs, sensory level, sphincters. Check perianal sensation and anal tone.
- Identify red flags: cancer history (metastatic compression), fever, recent infection or a recent spinal procedure (epidural abscess), anticoagulation (epidural hematoma), trauma.
- Order an emergency MRI of the whole spine if the level is uncertain. Metastatic disease is often multilevel.
- In suspected malignant cord compression, corticosteroids are commonly started (per local protocol) and oncology and spine surgery are involved early; definitive treatment may be surgical decompression and stabilization followed by radiotherapy, which outperforms radiotherapy alone in selected patients.
- Epidural abscess needs urgent drainage in most patients with neurological deficits plus prolonged antibiotics.

**Degenerative cervical myelopathy**: often presents insidiously with hand clumsiness, trouble with buttons, gait imbalance and Hoffmann signs. The mJOA score grades severity. Moderate and severe disease generally warrants decompression; mild disease may be managed with close monitoring or surgery depending on progression. Neck manipulation should be avoided.

**Traps**
- A thoracic sensory level with a cervical lesion: sensory levels can lie several segments below the true lesion.
- Guillain-Barré syndrome can mimic acute myelopathy; preserved bladder function and areflexia favor GBS, but there is overlap.
- Normal brain MRI in a patient with "progressive MS-like" leg weakness: image the spine, and consider a dural AV fistula, which can be missed unless flow voids are sought.
- Functional weakness can coexist with real cord compression; examine carefully before attributing deficits.

keyPoints: Myelopathy: UMN signs below the level, sensory level, sphincter dysfunction.
Landmarks: nipple T4, umbilicus T10, groin L1.
Brown-Séquard: ipsilateral weakness and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss.
Anterior cord syndrome spares vibration and proprioception (posterior spinal arteries).
Cauda equina: LMN, asymmetric, radicular pain; conus: early sphincter loss, mixed signs.
Acute compression (metastasis, abscess, hematoma) is a neurosurgical emergency: urgent MRI.

lessons.title: Radiculopathy

levels.kid:
Nerves leave the spinal cord through little doors between the bones of your back. These nerve roots are like branches coming off a tree trunk.

Sometimes a soft cushion between the bones, called a disc, bulges out and presses on a root. Ouch! The pain can shoot down the arm or the leg in a stripe, along the path that root takes care of.

The skin has a map of stripes, one stripe for each root. If a doctor knows where the pain, the numbness and the weak muscle are, they can tell which root is being pinched, like knowing which branch is shaking the leaves.
levels.hs:
A **radiculopathy** is a problem with a single **nerve root** as it leaves the spine. It is often caused by a **herniated disc** or by bony narrowing (**spinal stenosis**) pinching the root.

Typical features:
- **Radiating pain** down an arm or leg (**sciatica** in the leg), often worse with coughing, sneezing or certain positions
- Numbness or tingling in a **dermatome** (the strip of skin supplied by that root)
- Weakness of muscles supplied by that root (its **myotome**)
- A reduced reflex for that root

Common ones:
- **C6**: pain to the thumb, weak biceps/wrist extension, reduced biceps or brachioradialis reflex
- **C7**: pain to the middle finger, weak triceps, reduced triceps reflex
- **L4**: shin numbness, weak knee extension, reduced knee reflex
- **L5**: numbness on top of the foot and big toe, weak big-toe lift (foot drop), no standard reflex
- **S1**: numbness of the sole and little toe, weak push-off, reduced ankle reflex

In the lower back, the disc between L4 and L5 usually pinches the **L5 root**, and the L5–S1 disc usually pinches **S1**.

Most disc problems improve with time, activity and physical therapy. Surgery is considered for severe or worsening weakness, pain that does not improve, or **red flags** like bladder problems (cauda equina syndrome), which need emergency care.
levels.college:
**Clinical definition**: dysfunction of a spinal nerve root producing dermatomal sensory symptoms, myotomal weakness, reflex changes and radicular pain. Because roots are LMN pathways, weakness is lower motor neuron in type, and UMN signs are absent unless the cord is also compressed (myeloradiculopathy).

**Cervical numbering**: cervical roots exit ABOVE the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra (C6 exits at C5–C6) and C8 exits at C7–T1. Thus a C5–C6 disc compresses the C6 root. In the lumbar spine, roots exit BELOW the same-numbered pedicle; a typical posterolateral (paracentral) L4–L5 disc compresses the traversing L5 root, while a far lateral (foraminal) L4–L5 disc compresses the exiting L4 root.

**Root table**
- C5: deltoid, biceps; lateral arm; biceps reflex
- C6: biceps, wrist extensors; thumb and index; brachioradialis/biceps
- C7: triceps, wrist flexors, finger extensors; middle finger; triceps reflex
- C8: finger flexors, intrinsics; little finger and medial forearm
- L4: quadriceps, tibialis anterior; medial leg; patellar reflex
- L5: extensor hallucis longus, hip abduction, foot inversion and eversion; dorsum of foot
- S1: gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus; lateral foot and sole; Achilles reflex

**Provocative signs**: Spurling test (neck extension and rotation toward the symptomatic side reproduces arm pain) for cervical radiculopathy; straight leg raise (pain radiating below the knee between about 30 and 70 degrees) for L5/S1; femoral stretch for L2–L4.

**Differential**: peripheral nerve lesions (median, ulnar, peroneal), plexopathy, shoulder or hip disease, herpes zoster (dermatomal pain before the rash), diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy, and tumors.

**Investigations**: MRI if red flags, progressive deficit, or persistent pain beyond about 6 weeks with surgery under consideration; EMG distinguishes root from nerve lesions (paraspinal denervation and normal sensory nerve action potentials point to the root, because the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion).
levels.phd:
Radicular pain is more than mechanical pressure. Experimental compression of a normal root produces numbness and paresthesia, but pain requires inflammation: nucleus pulposus material contains TNF-α, IL-1β, phospholipase A2 and other mediators that sensitize the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) and root, generating ectopic discharges. This explains why the size of a disc herniation on MRI correlates poorly with symptoms, and why many herniations, especially large sequestered ones, regress spontaneously as macrophages resorb the extruded material.

**The DRG as a key structure.** The DRG lies within or just lateral to the foramen. Lesions proximal to it (preganglionic, e.g. root avulsions, intraspinal disc herniations) leave the peripheral sensory axon attached to its cell body, so sensory nerve action potentials remain normal despite clinical sensory loss. This electrophysiological signature differentiates radiculopathy from plexopathy or neuropathy.

**Myotome overlap.** Most muscles receive innervation from two or more roots, so single-root lesions rarely cause complete paralysis; they cause partial weakness in a distinctive combination. Dermatomes overlap even more, and their maps differ among historical sources (Foerster, Keegan and Garrett), which is why sensory findings are less reliable than motor and reflex findings for level determination.

**Natural history and evidence.** Most lumbar radiculopathies improve over weeks to months. Randomized trials (e.g. the SPORT trial) found faster relief with discectomy, but outcomes often converged over longer follow-up in intention-to-treat analyses, with significant crossover complicating interpretation. Epidural steroid injections provide short-term relief in some patients, with modest long-term benefit. Prognosis depends on psychosocial factors, central sensitization and occupational context as well as anatomy.

**Anatomical variation.** Conjoined nerve roots, furcal nerves (L4 contributing to both femoral and obturator nerves and to the lumbosacral trunk), and prefixed or postfixed plexuses alter clinical patterns and must be anticipated in surgical planning.
levels.expert:
Radiculopathy is the bread and butter of spine practice. The senior skill is matching the clinical root to the imaging level, then deciding who needs an operation.

**History and exam that change management**: dermatomal distribution of pain below the knee or elbow, precise myotomal weakness (big-toe extension and hip abduction for L5, single-leg calf raises and toe walking for S1), reflex asymmetry, straight leg raise and crossed straight leg raise (pain in the symptomatic leg when raising the other leg, highly specific for disc herniation).

**Correlation**: imaging abnormalities are extremely common in people without symptoms. Operate on the patient whose symptoms, exam and imaging all agree. If an MRI shows an L4–L5 disc but the patient has S1 findings, search for a second problem or an anatomical variation before booking surgery.

**Indications for surgery**
- Emergency: cauda equina syndrome (urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral symptoms) or rapidly progressive motor deficit.
- Urgent: profound or worsening foot drop.
- Elective: disabling pain persisting despite good nonoperative care, typically after 6 to 12 weeks, in a patient whose goals favor faster relief.

Options include microdiscectomy for lumbar herniation, and anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, cervical disc replacement, or posterior foraminotomy for cervical radiculopathy. Each has distinct complications (dural tear, recurrent herniation, dysphagia after anterior cervical approaches, adjacent-segment disease after fusion).

**Pitfalls**
- Missing a peripheral nerve lesion: foot drop with normal inversion is peroneal, not L5.
- Missing a myelopathy hiding behind arm radiculopathy.
- Missing malignancy or infection in a patient with night pain, weight loss or fever.
- Over-reliance on dermatome maps; motor and reflex findings localize better.

keyPoints: Radiculopathy = single root: dermatomal pain/numbness, myotomal LMN weakness, reduced reflex.
C6: thumb, biceps/brachioradialis; C7: middle finger, triceps; S1: lateral foot, ankle reflex.
L4–L5 paracentral disc → L5 root; L5–S1 → S1; far lateral disc hits the exiting root.
Cervical roots exit above their vertebra (C5–C6 disc → C6).
Sensory nerve action potentials are normal in radiculopathy (lesion proximal to DRG).
Cauda equina symptoms and progressive weakness are surgical red flags.

lessons.title: Plexus & Peripheral Nerve

levels.kid:
After the nerve roots leave your spine, they meet and mix like roads at a big tangled interchange. This interchange is called a plexus. There is one near your shoulder for your arm and one low in your belly for your leg.

Out of the plexus come the nerves, long wires that travel all the way to your fingers and toes.

Each nerve has its own job and its own patch of skin. If one nerve gets squished, like when your arm falls asleep, only its own patch goes numb or weak. Doctors use those patches like a map to figure out which wire has the problem.
levels.hs:
After leaving the spine, nerve roots join into networks called **plexuses** before splitting into named **peripheral nerves**:
- **Brachial plexus** (C5–T1) for the arm
- **Lumbosacral plexus** (L1–S4) for the leg

**Peripheral nerve lesions** cause weakness and numbness in that nerve's specific territory, which does not match a single dermatome.

Common examples:
- **Median nerve** (carpal tunnel syndrome): numbness of the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger, often worse at night; weak thumb muscles.
- **Ulnar nerve** (at the elbow): numbness of the little finger and half the ring finger; weak small hand muscles and a weak grip.
- **Radial nerve** (often from pressure on the upper arm): **wrist drop**, with numbness on the back of the hand near the thumb.
- **Common peroneal (fibular) nerve** (at the knee, from crossing the legs or a tight cast): **foot drop** and numbness on the top of the foot.

**Plexus lesions** affect several nerves and several roots at once. Examples include birth injuries (Erb palsy, upper trunk C5–C6, the "waiter's tip" position), motorcycle injuries, tumors at the top of the lung, and inflammation (brachial neuritis, with severe shoulder pain followed by weakness).

**Polyneuropathy** affects many nerves, usually symmetrically and starting in the feet. Diabetes is the most common cause.
levels.college:
**Localization strategy**: compare the deficit with root, plexus and nerve maps. A lesion that spans multiple nerves but within a single root is radicular; one that spans multiple nerves and roots is plexus; one confined to a nerve's territory, especially distal to a known branch, is a mononeuropathy.

**Brachial plexus anatomy**: roots (C5–T1) → trunks (upper C5–C6, middle C7, lower C8–T1) → divisions → cords (lateral, posterior, medial) → terminal nerves (musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar).
- **Upper trunk (Erb)**: shoulder abduction, external rotation and elbow flexion weak; arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, wrist flexed ("waiter's tip").
- **Lower trunk (Klumpke)**: hand intrinsics weak, claw hand, possible Horner syndrome if T1 is avulsed proximally; causes include apical lung tumors (Pancoast) and thoracic outlet syndrome.
- **Neuralgic amyotrophy** (Parsonage-Turner): acute severe pain followed by patchy weakness and wasting.

**Key mononeuropathies**
- **Median at wrist**: weak abductor pollicis brevis and opponens, sensory loss in the radial three and a half fingers, sparing the thenar eminence skin (palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel). Tinel and Phalen tests are supportive.
- **Ulnar at elbow**: weak interossei, hypothenar muscles and adductor pollicis (Froment sign), sensory loss of little and half the ring finger, including the dorsal hand (dorsal cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist).
- **Radial at spiral groove**: wrist and finger drop, triceps usually spared (branches arise more proximally).
- **Common fibular at fibular head**: weak dorsiflexion and eversion, inversion spared.
- **Femoral**: weak knee extension and hip flexion (if proximal), absent knee jerk, anteromedial thigh and medial leg numbness.

**Polyneuropathy patterns**: length-dependent sensorimotor (diabetes, toxins and chemotherapy, B12, hereditary), small-fiber (painful, normal reflexes), demyelinating (acquired, e.g. Guillain-Barré and CIDP), and **mononeuritis multiplex** (stepwise multiple mononeuropathies from vasculitis).
levels.phd:
Peripheral nerve injury is classified by structure, and structure predicts recovery.

**Seddon and Sunderland.** Neurapraxia (Sunderland I) is focal conduction block, often from demyelination, with full recovery in weeks. Axonotmesis (II–IV) disrupts axons with variably preserved endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium; Wallerian degeneration follows and regrowth proceeds at roughly a millimeter per day, so recovery depends on distance to target. Neurotmesis (V) is complete transection requiring surgical repair. Mixed injuries are common.

**Wallerian degeneration.** After axotomy the distal axon fragments over days through a programmed process regulated by SARM1 activation and loss of NMNAT2, a pathway now being studied as a therapeutic target to protect axons in neuropathies. Schwann cells dedifferentiate into repair cells, form bands of Büngner and guide regeneration. Prolonged denervation leads to loss of the Schwann cell repair phenotype and irreversible muscle fibrosis, which is why reinnervation beyond roughly 12 to 18 months rarely restores useful function.

**Electrodiagnosis.** Conduction block appears as a drop in compound muscle action potential amplitude across a segment; axonal loss reduces amplitudes distal to the lesion only after Wallerian degeneration has occurred (several days), so very early studies can mislead. Fibrillation potentials appear after about 2 to 3 weeks. Sensory nerve action potentials distinguish preganglionic from postganglionic lesions, crucial in brachial plexus trauma: normal SNAPs in an anesthetic limb indicate root avulsion.

**Demyelinating neuropathies.** Guillain-Barré syndrome can follow infection through molecular mimicry (e.g. Campylobacter lipooligosaccharide resembling gangliosides, producing anti-GM1 or anti-GQ1b antibodies). Antibodies to nodal and paranodal proteins (neurofascin-155, contactin-1) define "nodopathies" that respond differently to treatment, showing how molecular anatomy at the node of Ranvier is reshaping classification.

**Entrapment physiology.** Chronic compression produces focal demyelination and intraneural ischemia; the "double crush" hypothesis proposes that a proximal lesion makes a distal segment more vulnerable, though evidence remains debated.
levels.expert:
Peripheral nerve surgery is a precise subspecialty, and its decisions hinge on the exam and the clock.

**Exam essentials**: map the sensory loss carefully (autonomous zones are the most reliable, e.g. the pulp of the index finger for median, the little finger tip for ulnar), test individual muscles that distinguish neighboring nerves and roots (abductor pollicis brevis vs first dorsal interosseous separates median from ulnar; tibialis posterior separates L5 from peroneal), and check Tinel sign along the nerve course to follow regeneration.

**Timing decisions**
- Sharp laceration with deficit: early exploration and primary repair, ideally within days.
- Blunt or stretch injury with nerve in continuity: wait and watch for recovery with serial exam and electrodiagnostic studies at about 3 months; if there is no reinnervation, explore, use intraoperative nerve action potentials, and then repair, graft or transfer.
- Brachial plexus avulsion: root avulsions cannot be repaired directly; nerve transfers (e.g. spinal accessory to suprascapular, ulnar fascicle to biceps branch in the Oberlin transfer) restore key functions and must be done before muscle end-plates are lost.

**Entrapment management**: carpal tunnel release for persistent or severe median neuropathy (thenar wasting is a sign not to wait), ulnar decompression or transposition for cubital tunnel, and peroneal decompression at the fibular head. Always check for diabetes, hypothyroidism and other systemic contributors.

**Pitfalls**
- Calling a radial neuropathy a stroke: wrist drop with intact finger abduction once the wrist is supported, normal reflexes elsewhere and no UMN signs is peripheral.
- Missing Guillain-Barré syndrome in a patient with rising weakness and lost reflexes; monitor vital capacity and swallowing, because respiratory failure can come fast.
- Missing vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex, which requires urgent immunotherapy.
- Iatrogenic injury during positioning in surgery: padding and position checks prevent ulnar and peroneal palsies.

Radial nerve: wrist drop; common peroneal: foot drop with spared inversion.
Seddon: neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis; axons regrow about a millimeter a day.
Normal SNAPs with sensory loss suggest root avulsion (preganglionic).

lessons.title: Junction & Muscle

levels.kid:
At the very end of a nerve, there is a tiny gap before the muscle. The nerve sends a chemical message across the gap, like tossing a ball to a friend. When the muscle catches it, it squeezes.

In some illnesses, the muscle's catching mitts get blocked. The muscle works at first, then gets tired fast. Eyelids may droop, and things can look double by the evening.

In other illnesses, the muscle itself is the problem. Then the big muscles near the shoulders and hips get weak, so climbing stairs or lifting arms to brush hair gets hard. Feeling stays normal, because the feeling nerves are fine.
levels.hs:
The last two stops in the motor pathway are the **neuromuscular junction (NMJ)** and the **muscle** itself. Both cause weakness with **normal sensation**, which helps separate them from nerve problems.

**Neuromuscular junction disorders**
- The nerve releases **acetylcholine**, which binds receptors on the muscle.
- In **myasthenia gravis**, antibodies attack these receptors. The hallmark is **fatigable weakness**: it gets worse with use and better with rest. Droopy eyelids (ptosis) and double vision are common first signs, and weakness of swallowing or breathing can be dangerous (**myasthenic crisis**).
- **Lambert-Eaton syndrome**: antibodies block calcium channels on the nerve ending, so less acetylcholine is released. Leg weakness, dry mouth and reduced reflexes are typical; it is often linked to lung cancer.
- **Botulism**: a toxin blocks acetylcholine release, causing descending paralysis.

**Muscle disorders (myopathies)**
- Weakness is usually **proximal** (shoulders, hips) and symmetric: trouble climbing stairs, rising from a chair or lifting arms.
- Reflexes are usually normal until weakness is severe.
- Causes include inherited muscular dystrophies (e.g. Duchenne), inflammatory myositis, thyroid problems and some medicines (like statins, rarely).
- A blood test for **creatine kinase (CK)**, a muscle enzyme, is often high.

Neither type causes numbness. That is a key clue.
levels.college:
**Clinical separation of the lower motor unit**
- **Neuropathy**: distal weakness, sensory loss, reduced reflexes.
- **NMJ**: fatigable, fluctuating weakness, often ocular and bulbar; normal sensation; reflexes normal (myasthenia) or reduced with post-exercise facilitation (Lambert-Eaton).
- **Myopathy**: proximal symmetric weakness, no sensory loss, reflexes preserved until late; CK often elevated.

**Myasthenia gravis**: antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor (AChR, most patients), MuSK or LRP4 reduce the safety factor of transmission. Signs: fatigable ptosis (sustained upgaze), diplopia, bulbar weakness, neck flexor and proximal limb weakness. Tests: antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement), single-fiber EMG (increased jitter), and CT chest for thymoma. Treatment classes: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine), immunosuppression, complement and FcRn inhibitors, thymectomy, and plasma exchange or IVIG for crisis. Many drugs worsen myasthenia (some antibiotics, magnesium, certain beta-blockers).

**Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome**: antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels; proximal leg weakness, autonomic symptoms, areflexia with facilitation after brief exercise; associated with small cell lung cancer in about half.

**Botulism**: toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking acetylcholine release; descending paralysis with dilated pupils.

**Myopathies**
- **Inflammatory**: dermatomyositis (skin rash), immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (very high CK, sometimes anti-HMGCR after statins), inclusion body myositis (finger flexor and quadriceps weakness, older adults, poor treatment response).
- **Dystrophies**: Duchenne (dystrophin absence, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign), myotonic dystrophy (distal weakness, myotonia, cataracts, cardiac conduction disease).
- **Metabolic and toxic**: hypothyroidism, glycogen and lipid storage disorders, corticosteroid myopathy (normal CK).

**Workup**: CK, EMG (short, small, polyphasic motor units with early recruitment in myopathy), MRI of muscle, biopsy, antibody panels and genetic testing.
levels.phd:
The neuromuscular junction is engineered with a large **safety factor**: under normal conditions each nerve impulse releases far more acetylcholine than needed to depolarize the end-plate to threshold, and acetylcholinesterase rapidly terminates the signal. Disease reduces this margin, and clinical weakness appears when repeated activity depletes readily releasable vesicles and transmission fails at some fibers.

**Mechanisms in myasthenia.** AChR antibodies (mostly IgG1 and IgG3) act through complement-mediated destruction of the postsynaptic membrane, cross-linking and accelerated internalization of receptors, and to a lesser degree direct channel blockade. The resulting simplified postsynaptic folds and reduced receptor density lower end-plate potentials. MuSK antibodies (mostly IgG4, which does not fix complement) disrupt the agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling that clusters receptors, explaining different clinical features (bulbar predominance, atrophy) and different treatment responses, including poorer response to cholinesterase inhibitors and good response to B-cell depletion.

**Decrement and facilitation.** Repetitive stimulation at low frequency (3 Hz) progressively depletes vesicle stores; in myasthenia this produces a decrementing response as end-plate potentials fall below threshold. In Lambert-Eaton, high-frequency stimulation or brief maximal exercise builds up residual presynaptic calcium, increasing release and producing marked facilitation of compound muscle action potentials.

**Muscle disease biology.** Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton to the dystroglycan complex and extracellular matrix; its absence makes the sarcolemma fragile under contraction, causing repeated necrosis and regeneration until satellite cell capacity is exhausted and fibrosis dominates. Therapeutic strategies include exon skipping (antisense oligonucleotides that restore the reading frame), gene therapy delivering micro-dystrophin, and corticosteroids. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 results from a CTG repeat expansion in DMPK; RNA with expanded repeats sequesters muscleblind-like splicing regulators, causing widespread missplicing (e.g. of the chloride channel CLCN1, producing myotonia), a paradigm of RNA toxicity.
levels.expert:
Junction and muscle disorders fill neuromuscular clinics and intensive care units, and they reward a careful bedside approach.

**Bedside techniques**: sustained upgaze for 60 seconds (ptosis or diplopia emerging), counting aloud on one breath, neck flexion strength (often weak in myasthenia and myopathy), repeated arm abduction to test fatigability, ice pack test on a ptotic eyelid (improvement suggests myasthenia), observation of rising from a squat (Gowers sign), and checking for myotonia (slow hand opening after a firm grip).

**Respiratory monitoring**: in myasthenic crisis or Guillain-Barré syndrome, track forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force regularly. Oxygen saturation drops late; do not rely on it. Bulbar weakness threatens the airway before the lungs fail. The "20-30-40 rule", a set of thresholds for vital capacity and maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures, is a commonly cited prompt to consider intubation.

**Medication safety**: before starting new drugs in myasthenia, check whether they can worsen transmission (fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, magnesium, some anesthetic agents). Anesthesiologists must know the diagnosis because neuromuscular blocking agents behave unpredictably.

**Thymus surgery**: thymectomy benefits many patients with AChR-antibody generalized myasthenia (supported by the MGTX trial) and is mandatory for thymoma. Patients are optimized beforehand, sometimes with plasma exchange or IVIG.

**Myopathy pearls**
- A very high CK with progressive proximal weakness in someone on a statin who does not improve after stopping it suggests anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy, which needs immunotherapy.
- Dermatomyositis in adults warrants cancer screening.
- Check the heart in dystrophies (cardiomyopathy and conduction disease are major causes of death).
- Steroid myopathy is a common hospital cause of new proximal weakness with a normal CK.

**Surgical overlap**: neurosurgeons and spine surgeons must recognize neuromuscular disease, because unexplained weakness after surgery or difficulty weaning from ventilation may reflect an undiagnosed junction or muscle disorder.

keyPoints: NMJ and muscle disorders cause weakness with normal sensation.
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and proximal weakness; AChR antibodies.
Lambert-Eaton: presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, areflexia with post-exercise facilitation, linked to small cell lung cancer.
Myopathy: proximal symmetric weakness, normal reflexes until late, often high CK.
Repetitive stimulation: decrement in myasthenia, increment in Lambert-Eaton.
Monitor vital capacity in myasthenic crisis; oxygen saturation falls late.

lessons.title: Peripheral Cases

levels.kid:
Time for more detective work, this time outside the brain!

Case 1: A girl's thumb and first fingers tingle at night after lots of drawing. Only those fingers. Clue: one nerve at the wrist is squeezed!

Case 2: A man has back pain that shoots down one leg to his foot. Clue: a stripe of pain means a pinched root in the back.

Case 3: A lady's eyelids droop and her eyes see double, but only when she is tired at night. Her feeling is normal. Clue: the tiny gap between nerve and muscle is tired.

Each clue points to a different spot, just like a map.
levels.hs:
Practice placing the lesion below the brain.

**Case 1.** A 45-year-old has numbness and tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night. Her thumb muscles look thin.
- Where: median nerve at the wrist.
- What: carpal tunnel syndrome.

**Case 2.** A 38-year-old lifts a heavy box and develops back pain shooting down the back of his leg to the sole. His ankle reflex is gone and calf raises are weak.
- Where: S1 nerve root.
- What: L5–S1 disc herniation.

**Case 3.** A 25-year-old develops tingling in the feet, then weakness rising up the legs over a week, after a stomach bug. Reflexes are absent.
- Where: many peripheral nerves (polyradiculoneuropathy).
- What: Guillain-Barré syndrome; breathing must be monitored.

**Case 4.** A 30-year-old has double vision and droopy eyelids that get worse through the day; sensation and reflexes are normal.
- Where: neuromuscular junction.
- What: myasthenia gravis.

**Case 5.** A 55-year-old has trouble climbing stairs and raising her arms, with a purple rash on her eyelids and knuckles. Sensation is normal and CK is high.
- Where: muscle.
- What: dermatomyositis.

Key questions each time: Is sensation involved? Is it one nerve's pattern, one root's stripe, or symmetric? Are reflexes lost? Is the weakness fatigable or proximal?
levels.college:
**Case A.** Progressive symmetric weakness over 10 days after diarrheal illness; distal paresthesias; areflexia; bilateral facial weakness; normal sensation on exam except mild vibration loss. CSF: high protein, normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation). Nerve conduction: demyelinating features. Localization: roots and peripheral nerves diffusely. Diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP). Management: monitor vital capacity, autonomic instability; IVIG or plasma exchange.

**Case B.** Painless wasting of the right hand intrinsics, weak finger abduction and thumb adduction, numbness of the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger including the dorsal hand; normal median-innervated thenar muscles. Localization: ulnar nerve at or above the elbow (dorsal cutaneous involvement excludes Guyon canal). If thenar muscles and medial forearm sensation were also involved, consider C8/T1 root or lower trunk (e.g. Pancoast tumor, especially with Horner).

**Case C.** A diabetic patient develops severe thigh pain, then weakness of hip flexion, knee extension and hip adduction, with weight loss. Several nerves (femoral and obturator) and roots are involved: lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy). Usually monophasic with slow, incomplete recovery.

**Case D.** Stepwise painful foot drop on the left, then wrist drop on the right over months, with systemic symptoms. Multiple separate nerves in different limbs: mononeuritis multiplex. Search for vasculitis; nerve biopsy may be needed.

**Case E.** Slowly progressive asymmetric hand weakness with fasciculations, brisk reflexes in the same limb, no sensory loss. Mixed UMN and LMN signs: motor neuron disease (ALS) versus cervical myeloradiculopathy, which must be excluded by MRI.

**Case F.** Fatigable ptosis and dysphagia, normal reflexes; CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Myasthenia gravis with thymoma; thymectomy indicated.

**Framework**: sensory involvement (yes → nerve, root, plexus; no → anterior horn, NMJ, muscle), distribution (single nerve, root, plexus, length-dependent, multifocal), reflexes, fatigability, tempo and associated features.
levels.phd:
Peripheral localization becomes difficult when diseases straddle compartments or evolve in time, and these cases illustrate the reasoning.

**The pure motor syndrome.** Asymmetric weakness without sensory loss can arise at the anterior horn (motor neuron disease), the motor root, the motor nerve (multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block), the NMJ or the muscle. Multifocal motor neuropathy, with anti-GM1 IgM antibodies and conduction block on electrodiagnosis, mimics ALS but responds to IVIG, making electrodiagnostic search for conduction block essential before diagnosing ALS. Fasciculations and UMN signs favor ALS; weakness in a nerve distribution with preserved bulk early favors MMN.

**Acute flaccid weakness.** The differential spans Guillain-Barré syndrome, acute myelopathy (early spinal shock mimics LMN weakness), botulism, myasthenic crisis, periodic paralysis, critical illness neuropathy and myopathy, and acute flaccid myelitis in children (anterior horn involvement linked to enterovirus D68). Sphincter involvement, a sensory level and pupils (dilated in botulism) help separate these. CSF, MRI and electrodiagnosis resolve most cases.

**Time as a diagnostic axis.** GBS reaches its nadir within four weeks; progression beyond eight weeks defines CIDP, which needs maintenance immunotherapy. Acute-onset CIDP (A-CIDP) presents like GBS but relapses, and nodopathies (anti-neurofascin-155, anti-contactin-1) fall between these entities with distinct treatment responses.

**Multifocality and the plexus.** Neuralgic amyotrophy may involve nerves outside the brachial plexus (phrenic, anterior interosseous) and can have a hereditary form linked to SEPT9 mutations. High-resolution MRI and ultrasound have revealed hourglass-like constrictions of individual fascicles, reframing some idiopathic mononeuropathies as surgically treatable.

**Critical illness polyneuropathy and myopathy.** In ICU patients with sepsis and multiorgan failure, axonal neuropathy and myopathy (with loss of myosin filaments) cause failure to wean from ventilation. Distinguishing them requires direct muscle stimulation studies, and prevention focuses on glycemic control, minimizing sedation and early mobilization.
levels.expert:
Peripheral cases on the wards are usually urgent for one of two reasons: breathing or a surgical clock.

**Case: rising weakness in the emergency department.** A 40-year-old with tingling feet for three days now cannot climb stairs; reflexes are absent. Think GBS. Admit to a monitored bed, measure vital capacity every few hours, check swallowing and autonomic stability (heart rhythm and blood pressure swings), start IVIG or plasma exchange once the diagnosis is likely. Do not wait for the CSF protein to rise; it can be normal in the first week. Exclude cord compression with MRI if there is a sensory level or early sphincter involvement.

**Case: the foot drop referral.** A 50-year-old woke with a foot drop after a long surgery in the lithotomy position. Exam: weak dorsiflexion and eversion, normal inversion and plantarflexion, numb dorsum of foot, normal reflexes. Localization: common fibular nerve at the fibular head, likely compression during positioning. Plan: protect with an ankle-foot orthosis, electrodiagnostic study at about three weeks, and surgical exploration if no recovery over a few months. Had inversion and hip abduction been weak, the lesion would be L5 and MRI would come first.

**Case: hand weakness in the spine clinic.** A 60-year-old has hand clumsiness and wasting, a positive Hoffmann sign and brisk leg reflexes. Two possibilities: cervical myeloradiculopathy (surgically treatable) and ALS. MRI shows multilevel cervical stenosis with cord signal change. Even so, an EMG looking for widespread denervation (including thoracic paraspinals and tongue) is wise before surgery, because ALS patients may be offered an operation that cannot help them.

**Senior habits**: always ask "is there sensory involvement?", always check reflexes, always consider whether the diagnosis threatens breathing or swallowing, and always correlate imaging with the exam. Electrodiagnostic studies are an extension of the clinical exam, and their timing (days to weeks after injury) affects what they can show.

keyPoints: Ask first: is sensation involved? Yes → nerve/root/plexus; no → anterior horn, NMJ or muscle.
Distribution: single nerve, dermatome, plexus, length-dependent, or multifocal (mononeuritis multiplex).
Rising weakness with areflexia after infection = Guillain-Barré: monitor vital capacity.
Ulnar lesion with dorsal hand numbness = at/above elbow; add thenar weakness and Horner → C8/T1 or lower trunk.
Mixed UMN + LMN signs: ALS vs cervical myeloradiculopathy; EMG plus MRI.
Peroneal vs L5 foot drop: test inversion and hip abduction.
